question: What is the difference between an L4 and L7 load balancer?

options.text: L4 operates at the TCP/UDP level (sees only IP and port), while L7 parses HTTP requests (URL, headers, cookies)
options.explanation: L4 operates at the transport layer — forwards the TCP connection as a whole without looking inside. L7 parses the application protocol (HTTP) and can route by URL, headers, cookies. L4 is faster, L7 is smarter

options.text: L4 supports only 4 servers, while L7 supports up to 7
options.explanation: The numbers 4 and 7 refer to OSI model layers (Open Systems Interconnection), not the number of servers. L4 = transport layer (TCP/UDP), L7 = application layer (HTTP)

options.text: L7 is faster than L4 because it operates at a higher level
options.explanation: L4 is significantly faster than L7 (millions of packets/sec vs million requests/sec) because it doesn't need to parse packet contents. A higher level means more work, not more speed

options.text: L4 only works with HTTP, while L7 works with any protocol
options.explanation: The opposite: L4 works with any TCP/UDP protocol (without looking inside), while L7 specializes in HTTP/HTTPS and can inspect request contents

question: Which load balancing algorithm is best suited for a scenario where requests have highly varying processing times (from 10 ms to 5 seconds)?

options.text: Round Robin
options.explanation: Round Robin distributes requests evenly in rotation, without accounting for current load. A server that receives several 'heavy' 5-second requests will be overloaded while others idle

options.text: Least Connections
options.explanation: Least Connections directs a request to the server with the fewest active connections. A server processing heavy requests accumulates connections and receives fewer new ones — load automatically balances

options.text: IP Hash
options.explanation: IP Hash binds a client to a server by IP address hash. It accounts for neither load nor processing time — one 'heavy' client can overload its server

options.text: Weighted Round Robin
options.explanation: Weighted RR accounts for server capacity (weights), but not current load. If a powerful server receives a series of heavy requests, it will still be overloaded

question: What is the main advantage of consistent hashing over regular hash % N?

options.text: When adding/removing a server, only ~1/N keys move, not all of them
options.explanation: With hash % N, changing the number of servers redistributes ~75-100% of keys. With consistent hashing — only ~1/N (keys between the new and previous server on the ring). This is critical for caches and sharded systems

options.text: Consistent hashing guarantees perfectly even distribution
options.explanation: Without virtual nodes, consistent hashing can produce uneven distribution. Virtual nodes (100-200 per server) are needed precisely for balancing. The main advantage is minimal redistribution when server count changes

options.text: Consistent hashing is faster to compute
options.explanation: Consistent hashing has O(log N) complexity for finding the right server on the ring, while hash % N is O(1). Speed is not its advantage

options.text: Consistent hashing doesn't require knowing the number of servers in advance
options.explanation: Regular hash % N also doesn't require knowing the server count in advance — N is substituted at computation time. The advantage of consistent hashing is minimal data redistribution

question: Which statements about health checks are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Active health checks — the load balancer periodically polls servers itself
options.explanation: Active health checks send HTTP requests (usually GET /health) to servers every N seconds. This enables fast failure detection, even if the server receives no real traffic

options.text: Best practice — use both active and passive health checks simultaneously
options.explanation: Active checks provide fast detection (seconds), passive provide additional insurance without overhead. Together they give maximum reliability

options.text: Passive health checks track errors in real responses to clients
options.explanation: Passive checks observe the results of real requests. If a server starts returning 5xx errors or timeouts, it's removed from the pool. Pros — zero overhead, cons — first clients get errors

options.text: None of the above options are correct
options.explanation: Some of the listed options are indeed correct.

options.text: Health check endpoint should return 200 OK if the process is running
options.explanation: A health check should verify real readiness: DB availability, Redis, sufficient disk space. The process may be running but unable to serve requests (DB down, disk full)

question: Why are sticky sessions considered an anti-pattern for scalable systems?

options.text: Harder to scale horizontally — new servers don't receive traffic from bound clients
options.explanation: Existing clients continue hitting old servers. New servers only receive new clients, which slows load balancing during scaling

options.text: Sticky sessions are technically impossible to implement
options.explanation: Sticky sessions are easily implemented via IP hash, cookie-based affinity, or header-based routing. The problem isn't implementation, but the consequences for scalability and fault tolerance

options.text: Load is distributed unevenly due to 'hot' clients
options.explanation: One active client (or group of clients) can generate a disproportionately large load on its server while other servers idle

options.text: When a server goes down, all clients bound to it lose their state
options.explanation: Sticky sessions bind a client to a specific server. If that server fails, all its clients lose their sessions and data stored in server memory
